'''René Frédéric Thom''' ({{IPA|fr|ʁəne tɔm|lang}}; 2 September 1923 – 25 October 2002) was a French mathematician, who received the [[Fields Medal]] in 1958.

He made his reputation as a [[topologist]], moving on to aspects of what would be called [[singularity theory]]; he became world-famous among the wider academic community and the educated general public for one aspect of this latter interest, his work as the founder of [[catastrophe theory]] (later developed by [[Christopher Zeeman]]).<ref>{{MacTutor Biography|id=Thom}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Wright |first=Pearce |date=14 November 2002 |title=Obituary: René Thom |language=en |work=[[The Guardian]] |url=http://www.theguardian.com/news/2002/nov/14/guardianobituaries.highereducation1 |access-date=10 April 2022}} also available at {{Cite web |title=René Thom – Guardian obituary |url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Obituaries/Thom_Guardian/ |access-date=10 April 2022 |website=[[MacTutor History of Mathematics archive]] |publisher=[[University of St Andrews]] |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=René Frédéric Thom |url=https://www.encyclopedia.com/science/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/rene-frederic-thom |access-date=10 April 2022 |website=[[encyclopedia.com]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Alberganti |first=Michel |date=31 October 2002 |title=René Thom |language=fr |work=[[Le Monde]] |url=https://www.lemonde.fr/archives/article/2002/10/31/rene-thom_4246539_1819218.html |access-date=10 April 2022}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Thom René Frédéric |url=http://serge.mehl.free.fr/chrono/thom.html |access-date=10 April 2022 |website=serge.mehl.free.fr}}</ref>

== Life and career ==
René Thom grew up in a modest family in [[Montbéliard]], Doubs and obtained a [[Baccalauréat]] in 1940. After the [[German invasion of France (1940)|German invasion of France]], his family took refuge in Switzerland and then in [[Lyon]]. In 1941 he moved to Paris to attend [[Lycée Saint-Louis]] and in 1943 he began studying mathematics at [[École Normale Supérieure]], becoming [[agrégé]] in 1946.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Dougnac |first=Sophie |date=30 July 2015 |title=René Thom: le fils d'épiciers devient prix Nobel |trans-title=René Thom: the grocers' son becomes Nobel prize |url=https://www.estrepublicain.fr/actualite/2015/07/30/le-fils-d-epiciers-devient-prix-nobel |access-date=10 April 2022 |publisher=[[L'Est Républicain]] |language=FR-fr}}</ref>

He received his PhD in 1951 from the [[University of Paris]]. His thesis, titled ''Espaces fibrés en sphères et carrés de Steenrod'' (''Sphere bundles and Steenrod squares''), was written under the direction of [[Henri Cartan]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=René Thom – The Mathematics Genealogy Project |url=https://www.genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu/id.php?id=93398 |access-date=10 April 2022 |website=www.genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu}}</ref>

After a fellowship at [[Princeton University Graduate College]] (1951–1952), he became [[Maître de conférences]] at the Universities of [[Université Joseph Fourier|Grenoble]] (1953–1954) and [[University of Strasbourg|Strasbourg]] (1954–1963), where he was appointed Professor in 1957. In 1964 he moved to the [[Institut des Hautes Études Scientifiques]], in [[Bures-sur-Yvette]], where he worked until 1990.<ref>{{Cite web |title=René Thom, permanent professor from 1963 to 1990 – IHES |url=https://www.ihes.fr/en/professeur/rene-thom-2/ |access-date=10 April 2022 |website=www.ihes.fr}}</ref>

In 1958, Thom received the [[Fields Medal]] at the [[International Congress of Mathematicians]] in Edinburgh for the foundations of [[cobordism]] theory, which were already present in his thesis.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://www.mathunion.org/fileadmin/ICM/Proceedings/ICM1958/ICM1958.ocr.pdf |title=Proceedings of the International Congress of Mathematician 1958 |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] |year=1960 |editor-last=Todd |editor-first=John Arthur |editor-link=J. A. Todd |location=Cambridge |pages=248–255}}</ref> He was [[invited speaker at the International Congress of Mathematicians]] two more times: in 1970 in [[Nice]]<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://www.mathunion.org/fileadmin/ICM/Proceedings/ICM1970.2/ICM1970.2.ocr.pdf |title=Proceedings of the International Congress of Mathematician 1970 |publisher={{Interlanguage link|Gauthier-Villars|lt=Gauthier-Villars|fr}} |year=1971 |editor-first= |location=Paris |pages=257–265 |language=fr}}</ref> and 1983 in [[Warsaw]] (which he did not attend).<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://www.mathunion.org/fileadmin/ICM/Proceedings/ICM1983.1/ICM1983.1.ocr.pdf |title=Proceedings of the International Congress of Mathematician 1983 |publisher=[[Polish Scientific Publishers PWN]] |year=1984 |editor-last=Ciesielski |editor-first=Zbigniew |editor-link=Czesław Olech |location=Warsaw |pages=XVI |editor-last2=Olech |editor-first2=Czeslaw |editor-link2=Zbigniew Ciesielski}}</ref>

He was awarded the [[Brouwer Medal]] in 1970,<ref>{{Cite web |date=10 May 2017 |title=The Brouwer Lecture and the Brouwer Medal |url=http://www.utwente.nl/ewi/nmc2011/en/brouwer/ |access-date=10 April 2022 |website= |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170510094128/http://www.utwente.nl/ewi/nmc2011/en/brouwer/ |archive-date=10 May 2017 |url-status=dead}}</ref> the {{ill|Grand Prix Scientifique de la Ville de Paris|qid=Q139973376|s=1|v=sup}} in 1974, and the [[John von Neumann Lecture Prize]] in 1976.<ref>{{Cite web |title=SIAM: The John von Neumann Lecture |url=https://archive.siam.org/prizes/sponsored/vonneumann.php |access-date=10 April 2022 |publisher=[[Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics]] |archive-date=26 June 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210626184144/https://archive.siam.org/prizes/sponsored/vonneumann.php |url-status=dead }}</ref> He became the first president, together with [[Louis Néel]], of the newly established [[Fondation Louis-de-Broglie]] In 1973<ref>{{Cite web |title=Fondation Louis de Broglie |url=https://fondationlouisdebroglie.org/presentation.html |access-date=10 April 2022 |website=fondationlouisdebroglie.org}}</ref> and was elected Member of the [[Académie des Sciences]] of Paris in 1976.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Connes |first=Alain |author-link=Alain Connes |title=René Thom – Les Membres de l'Académie des sciences |url=https://www.academie-sciences.fr/archivage_site/academie/membre/Thom_Rene.htm |access-date=10 April 2022 |publisher=[[Académie des Sciences]]}}</ref>

[[Salvador Dalí]] paid homage to René Thom with the paintings ''[[The Swallow's Tail]]'' and ''Topological Abduction of Europe''.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Andrew |first=Masterson |date=16 January 2018 |title=René Thom: Dalí's favourite mathematician |url=https://cosmosmagazine.com/science/mathematics/rene-thom-dalis-favourite-mathematician/ |access-date=10 April 2022 |publisher=[[Cosmos (Australian magazine)|Cosmos]] |language=en-AU}}</ref>

== Research ==
While René Thom is most known to the public for his development of [[catastrophe theory]] between 1968 and 1972,<ref>[[E.C. Zeeman]], [http://www.gaianxaos.com/pdf/dynamics/zeeman-catastrophe_theory.pdf Catastrophe Theory], ''[[Scientific American]]'', April 1976; pp. 65–70, 75–83</ref> his academic achievements concern mostly his mathematical work on topology.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Hopf |first=Heinz |url=https://www.mathunion.org/fileadmin/ICM/Proceedings/ICM1958/ICM1958.ocr.pdf |title=The Work of R. Thom |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] |year=1960 |editor-first= |location=Cambridge |pages=X – XIV |language=de |author-link=Heinz Hopf}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=9 December 2019 |title=René Thom – Scholars |url=https://www.ias.edu/scholars/ren%C3%A9-thom |access-date=10 April 2022 |publisher=[[Institute for Advanced Study]] |language=en}}</ref>

In the early 1950s, it concerned what are now called [[Thom space]]s, [[characteristic class]]es, [[cobordism theory]], and the [[Thom transversality theorem]]. Another example of this line of work is the [[Thom conjecture]], versions of which have been investigated using [[gauge theory]]. From the mid 1950s he moved into [[singularity theory]], of which catastrophe theory is just one aspect, and in a series of deep (and at the time obscure) papers between 1960 and 1969 developed the theory of [[topologically stratified space|stratified sets]] and stratified maps, proving a basic stratified isotopy theorem describing the local conical structure of [[Whitney conditions|Whitney stratified sets]], now known as the [[Thom–Mather isotopy theorem]]. Much of his work on stratified sets was developed so as to understand the notion of topologically [[stable map]]s, and to eventually prove the result that the set of topologically stable mappings between two smooth manifolds is a [[dense set]].

Thom's lectures on the stability of differentiable mappings, given at the [[University of Bonn]] in 1960, were written up by [[Harold Levine]] and published in the proceedings of a year long symposium on singularities at [[Liverpool University]] during 1969–70, edited by [[C. T. C. Wall]]. The proof of the density of topologically stable mappings was completed by [[John Mather (mathematician)|John Mather]] in 1970, based on the ideas developed by Thom in the previous ten years. A coherent detailed account was published in 1976 by Christopher Gibson, Klaus Wirthmüller, Andrew du Plessis, and [[Eduard Looijenga]].<ref name="Gibson Wirthmüller Du Plessis Looijenga">{{cite book | last=Gibson | first=Christopher G. | last2=Wirthmüller | first2=Klaus | last3=Du Plessis | first3=Andrew | last4=Looijenga | first4=E. | title=Topological stability of smooth mappings | publisher=Springer-Verlag | publication-place=Berlin | date=1976 | isbn=3-540-07997-1 | oclc=2705384 | page=}}</ref>

During the last twenty years of his life Thom's published work was mainly in philosophy and epistemology, and he undertook a reevaluation of [[Aristotle]]'s writings on science. In 1992, he was one of eighteen academics who sent a letter to [[Cambridge University]] protesting against plans to award [[Jacques Derrida]] an honorary doctorate.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://ontology.buffalo.edu/smith/derridaletter.htm|title=Derrida Letter, The Cambridge Affair, 1992}}</ref>

Beyond Thom's contributions to algebraic topology, he studied differentiable mappings, through the study of [[Generic property|generic properties]]. In his final years, he turned his attention to an effort to apply his ideas about structural topography to the questions of thought, language, and meaning in the form of a "semiophysics".
